                                                                      cle pose, we randomly sample multiple nearby positions to
The T2P localization is formulated on local maps for prac-            serve as query locations. Each query location defines a pose
ticality. However, existing benchmark does not reflect the            cell, which represents the local region visible from that po-
scale and complexity of real-world environments. The most             sition. For each pose cell, all objects within S × S meters
widely used T2P localization benchmark, KITTI360Pose,                 area centered at the query location are collected, following
was designed for large-scale point cloud localization, yet            the same procedure used in map construction. A subset of
its submaps cover only small areas and contain a limited              Nt objects is then randomly selected to form the textual de-
number of simple objects. This substantially simplifies the           scription. For each selected object, its semantic label, color,
fine localization stage by restricting the search space and           and orientation relative to the pose cell are inserted into a
reducing scene clutter, yet diverges from the scenarios in            predefined template to generate the natural language query.
which humans typically perceive and describe much larger
and more complex surroundings [37, 60].                               4. Methodology

termines whether a textual object is groundable by comparing the

In parallel, the scene graph serves as a structured repre-             After obtaining the node–text correspondences by the PNA
sentation that connects semantic labels to pixel locations             module, VLM-Loc estimates the 2-DoF position ξ in pixel
and captures the relative spatial relationships among ob-              coordinates. We incorporate position prediction into the
jects, thereby bridging the BEV image and textual instruc-             autoregressive decoding, allowing the model to output the
tions. Together, the BEV image and scene graph allow the               corresponding 2D location on BEV image in the same se-
VLMs to exploit both fine-grained geometric cues and high-             quence of generation steps. This unified decoding strategy
level semantic relationships, facilitating precise spatial un-         allows the model to reason consistently from correspon-
derstanding and localization.                                          dences to spatial coordinates. The predicted pixel location
                                                                       is then converted to world coordinate system.
4.2. Partial Node Assignment
                                                                       4.4. Loss function
Although BEV images and scene graphs provide struc-
tured and complementary representations of the environ-                Following the autoregressive prediction paradigm of VLMs,
ment, T2P localization still faces two inherent challenges.            we train VLM-Loc by maximizing the likelihood of gener-
First, directly regressing coordinates from these inputs does          ating the correct text–node alignments and position predic-
not fully leverage the structured reasoning capability of              tions, both of which are expressed entirely in text form. For
VLMs, often resulting in ambiguous spatial interpretations.            each output token yt in the generated sequence, the training
Second, the map M covers only a limited region, some ob-               objective is the standard cross-entropy loss:
jects mentioned in the textual query may fall outside the
mapped area. As a result, only part of the mentioned ob-                          \mathcal {L} = -\sum _{t=1}^{T} \log P\!\left (y_t \mid y_{<t},\, s,\, \mathcal {T},\, I,\, \mathcal {G}\right ), \label {eq:loss}    (2)
jects can be grounded, which leads to a partial matching
problem that further complicates accurate pose estimation.

                                                                      11
     VLM-Loc: Localization in Point Cloud Maps via Vision-Language Models
                                              Supplementary Material
                                                                     B.1. CityLoc-K Construction
                                                                     Data source.       CityLoc-K is constructed based on the
                                                                     KITTI-360 dataset1 , which contains large-scale LiDAR
                                                                     point clouds collected by vehicle-mounted sensors along ur-
                                                                     ban roads in Karlsruhe. We use 5 training sequences (00,
                                                                     02, 04, 06, 07), 1 validation sequence (10), and 3 testing
                                                                     sequences (03, 05, 09).
                                                                     Map center sampling. When constructing the maps, we
                                                                     sample map centers from the vehicle trajectory. Specifi-
                            (a)                                      cally, we perform distance-based subsampling along the tra-
                                                                     jectory to ensure that any two selected centers are at least
                                                                     10 m apart. This ensures that sampling remains evenly dis-
                                                                     tributed across the entire trajectory, preventing points from
                                                                     clustering in specific regions and avoiding biased localiza-
                                                                     tion outcomes.
                                                                     Query location sampling. For each sampled map center,
                                                                     we further generate four query positions by randomly per-
                                                                     turbing its horizontal coordinates within ±15 m along both
                                                                     the East and North directions, thereby expanding the num-
                                                                     ber of query samples and positional diversity.
                            (b)                                      B.2. CityLoc-C Construction
Figure 6. Example point clouds from the CityLoc benchmark. (a)       Data source.         CityLoc-C is derived from SensatUr-
A roadside LiDAR scene from KITTI-360 [32]. (b) A photogram-         ban [20] and CityRefer [42]2 . For convenience, we denote
metric urban block from CityRefer [42].                              blocks in Birmingham and Cambridge as B# and C#, re-
                                                                     spectively. The dataset contains high-resolution photogram-
A. Overview                                                          metric point clouds with nearly three billion points collected
                                                                     across three UK cities, covering an area of 7.6 km2 . We use

C. Implementation Details                                                   ative direction. This approach allows us to construct infor-
C.1. Textual Query Generation                                               mative and scalable textual descriptions at minimal cost. It
                                                                            is fully free to generate, requires no LLMs, and avoids any
Components.      Each textual query T contains Nt hints.                    manual post-verification, while still preserving the key in-
Each hint h describes an object by specifying its color,                    formation necessary for fine-grained localization.
semantic category, and its directional relation with re-
spect to the query location, following the template for-                    C.2. System Prompt
mat: "The pose is <direction> of <color>                                    Our system prompt consists of six components designed to
<semantic>."                                                                guide the VLM in performing the T2P localization task, as
Direction computation.                For each object o referenced in       detailed in Tab. 7. The prompt could be formulated as :


                                                                        2
                                               Table 7. System prompt for VLM-Loc.

 You are a helpful assistant for spatial reasoning and grounding in BEV (bird’s-eye-view) images. You are also given
 a scene graph describing the environment as: {node id, label, pixel center}, where: - label = semantic label (e.g., “road”,
 “vegetation”, “building”, “pole”, etc.) - pixel center = pixel coordinates [x, y] (origin at top-left, x→right, y→down).

 COORDINATE & DIRECTION RULES: In BEV pixel coordinates: Up = North = y decreases; Down = South = y
 increases; Left = West = x decreases; Right = East = x increases.

 GOAL: (1) Parse the user’s natural-language description of a target location. (2) Extract all mentioned object phrases
 (e.g., “terrain”, “parking”) in order of appearance. (3) For each object phrase: Find the matching node in the given scene
 graph, determine whether grounding is successful (boolean), and record the matched node’s ID if grounded; otherwise
 set it to None. (4) Finally, infer the 2D pixel coordinate of the target location based on the described spatial relations
 (north/south/east/west/on-top).

 RULES: All reasoning and distance computation MUST be in pixel coordinates. Length of assignments MUST equal
 the number of mentioned objects in the user’s text. Each matched node id must exist in the scene graph; if not found or
 out of context, set ”grounded”: false and ”matched node”: None. Output exactly ONE JSON object in the schema below
 — no explanations, no extra text.

 OUTPUT FORMAT (STRICT): { ”assignments”: [ ”object label”: <string>, ”grounded”: <bool>, ”matched node”:
 <int|None>, ...], ”point 2d”: [<int>, <int>] }

 EXAMPLE (ILLUSTRATION ONLY): OUTPUT: { ”assignments”: [ ”object label”: ”parking”, ”grounded”: true,
 ”matched node”: 0, ”object label”: ”terrain”, ”grounded”: true, ”matched node”: 8, ”object label”: ”road”, ”grounded”:
 true, ”matched node”: 4, ”object label”: ”vegetation”, ”grounded”: true, ”matched node”: 11], ”point 2d”: [45, 135] }



• Role: specifies the localization task for the VLM and               • Example: provides a concrete example that illustrates the
  clearly defines the expected input structure, including the           predefined output format for the model to follow. Specif-
  types of information provided, their format, and the order            ically, the output should first present the visibility and as-
  in which they are supplied.                                           signment status for each textual hint, followed by the es-
• Coordinate system: provides the correspondence be-                    timated 2D pixel coordinates.
  tween the pixel coordinate system and the geospatial co-
  ordinate system, which is essential for enabling the model          D. Additional Experiments

The latency is acceptable for the T2P localization setting.
Moreover, the inference cost can be significantly reduced
via quantization, smaller backbones, and optimized deploy-
ment frameworks, making VLM-Loc more practical for
real-world systems.

E. Qualitative Results
Additional qualitative results of our approach and baselines
on the CityLoc-K and CityLoc-C splits are shown in Fig. 9
and Fig. 10. The results demonstrate the superior perfor-
mance of the proposed method over baselines across diverse
scenes, validating its robustness and accuracy.

respectively. The localization error is shown below each image, and green/red borders indicate localization error below/above 5 m.
